payload.excerpt: Wedding place card ideas grouped by style, from calligraphy and acrylic to keepsake stones and edible names, plus how to match names to the seating plan, keep cards readable and plan them for a wedding overseas.
key_takeaways: Shortlist from six style groups (classic paper, natural and edible, keepsakes, glass and acrylic, local touches, napkin or plate), then check your choice survives wind, heat and travel.
Take every name from one source, your finished seating plan, and check spelling, titles and preferred names before anything is made.
Edible place cards are food, so give your caterer the list of what is in them and of guests with allergies.
For a destination wedding, decide early whether the cards are made at home and carried or made near the venue, and who sets them out on the day.

faq.q: Do you need place cards if you have escort cards?
faq.a: Not always. If guests choose their own seat at an assigned table, escort cards alone can be enough. For a plated dinner with meal choices, place cards help the team serve each guest correctly.

faq.q: What goes on a wedding place card?
faq.a: The guest's name, written as they prefer to be addressed. Some couples add a meal choice symbol for the catering team.

faq.q: Who gets a place card at a wedding?
faq.a: Every guest with an assigned seat, children and the head table included.

faq.q: When should you order or make wedding place cards?
faq.a: After RSVPs close and the seating plan is settled, with room left for late changes and a proof.

faq.q: Can place cards double as wedding favours?
faq.a: Yes. Glassware, small stones, slate hearts, plants and edible cards all mark the seat and serve as the favour.

faq.q: What can I use instead of place cards?
faq.a: A name tag tied to the napkin, a card resting on the plate, a menu printed with each guest's name, or lettering on the wine glass all do the same job as wedding name cards.
